section.title: The Lord Is My Strength and My Shield
section.sectionRationale: A psalm of David that moves from urgent lament, pleading that God not stay silent, into a prayer for justice against those who speak peace while hiding malice, and then turns to praise for being heard, closing with intercession for God's anointed king and His people as a flock to be shepherded and carried forever.
section.thesis: David's cry that God not remain silent turns, upon being heard, into praise that the LORD is his strength and shield, grounding his closing prayer that God would shepherd and carry His people, and their anointed king, forever.
section.frameNote: Four movements: an urgent cry that God not remain silent (1-2); a plea for justice against those who speak peace while hiding malice (3-5); praise for being heard, the LORD as strength and shield (6-7); and intercession for God's anointed and His people, shepherded and carried forever (8-9).

units.label: Be not deaf to me, O my Rock
units.note: an urgent cry that God not remain silent

verses.text: To You, O LORD, I call; be not deaf to me, O my Rock. For if You remain silent, I will be like those descending to the Pit.
Hear my {{techinnah|cry for mercy}} when I call to You for help, when I lift up my hands toward Your holy sanctuary.

units.label: Repay them according to their deeds
units.note: a plea for justice against hidden malice

verses.text: Do not drag me away with the wicked, and with the workers of iniquity, who speak peace to their neighbors while malice is in their hearts.
Repay them according to their deeds and for their works of evil. Repay them for what their hands have done; bring back on them what they deserve.
Since they show no regard for the works of the LORD or what His hands have done, He will tear them down and never rebuild them.

units.label: The LORD is my strength and my shield

verses.text: Blessed be the LORD, for He has heard my cry for mercy.
The LORD is my strength and my shield; my heart trusts in Him, and I am helped. Therefore my heart rejoices, and I give thanks to Him with my song.

units.label: Shepherd them and carry them forever
units.note: intercession for the anointed and God's people

verses.text: The LORD is the strength of His people, a stronghold of salvation for His {{mashiach|anointed}}.
Save Your people and bless Your inheritance; {{roeh|shepherd}} them and carry them forever.

techinnah.gloss: A cry for mercy or supplication, from the root meaning to be gracious. It is the plea of one with no claim on God but His own gracious character, repeated in verse 6 when that plea is answered.

mashiach.gloss: Anointed one, the title given to Israel's king set apart by anointing oil for God's purposes. David prays for God's mashiach here as Israel's present king, a title and office that finds its ultimate fulfillment in Jesus, the Messiah, the Anointed One, Acts 2:36.

roeh.gloss: Shepherd, one who tends and carries a flock. David's closing prayer that God would shepherd and carry His people forever anticipates the LORD's own shepherding care fulfilled completely in Jesus, the good shepherd, John 10:11.

basic.context: David cries out that God not remain silent, fearing to become like those who go down to the Pit if his prayer goes unanswered. He prays for justice against those who speak peace to their neighbors while harboring malice, that they be repaid for their deeds. Then, upon being heard, David's tone shifts entirely to praise, the LORD as his strength and shield, and the psalm closes with intercession for God's anointed king and for His people as a flock to be shepherded and carried forever.
basic.hermeneutics: This psalm should be read as an honest model of prayer that moves from desperate plea to confident praise within a single breath, showing that being heard by God, not the removal of every threat, is what turns lament into thanksgiving.
basic.originalLanguages: David's techinnah, cry for mercy, appeals purely to God's gracious character. His closing prayer is for God's mashiach, His anointed king, and that the LORD would be ro'eh, shepherd, to His whole people, carrying them forever, imagery that finds its complete fulfillment in Jesus, God's true Anointed and Shepherd.
basic.typology: David's prayer for God's anointed, verse 8, anticipates the ultimate Anointed One, Jesus the Messiah, and his closing image of God shepherding and carrying His people forever, verse 9, anticipates the good shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep and carries them home, John 10:11, Isaiah 40:11.
basic.christ: Jesus is God's true mashiach, the Anointed One, whom Peter proclaims as both Lord and Christ, Acts 2:36, the fulfillment of David's prayer for God's anointed king in verse 8. And Jesus is the good shepherd David prays for in verse 9, who shepherds and carries His people not merely as a national blessing but by laying down His own life for the sheep, John 10:11, and gathering the lost and scattered into His own arms, Isaiah 40:11.
basic.god: God is shown as a rock who must not remain silent, whose justice repays hidden malice even when it hides behind pleasant words, and whose strength and shield become the ground of overflowing praise once His people know they have been heard.
basic.crossReferences: Acts 2:36 proclaims Jesus as both Lord and Christ, God's ultimate Anointed One, fulfilling David's prayer for God's mashiach in verse 8. John 10:11 shows Jesus as the good shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep, fulfilling the closing prayer of verse 9. Isaiah 40:11 pictures the LORD gathering lambs in His arms and carrying them close to His heart, the same shepherding hope David prays for God's people.
basic.oneStory: David's urgent cry that God not stay silent turns into praise once he is heard, and his closing prayer for God's anointed king and shepherded people finds its full and final answer in Jesus Christ, God's true Anointed One and good shepherd, who lays down His life for His flock and carries them home forever.

context.literary:
Psalm 28 turns on a single hinge between verses 5 and 6. Everything before it is petition, in the imperative and in the grammar of need: 'be not deaf', 'hear', 'do not drag me', 'repay them'. Everything after it is thanksgiving, in the perfect tense of a thing that has happened: 'He has heard my cry for mercy', 'I am helped'. The psalm does not narrate the answer. Between the last line of the curse and the first line of the blessing there is a silence in which the whole change takes place, and readers are left to imagine what happened.

The opening verse fixes what the poem is afraid of. The fear is not first of enemies but of God's silence: 'if You remain silent, I will be like those descending to the Pit.' The same word, silent, is the thing that is overcome in verse 6, so the psalm both opens and turns on God's speech. Verse 2 carries the body of the prayer with lifted hands and the sanctuary in view, and it supplies the picture of a person praying toward the place where God has promised to hear.

The middle section, verses 3 to 5, has its own shape. It begins with the wicked who 'speak peace' with malice underneath, moves through a threefold request for repayment (their deeds, their works, what their hands have done), and finishes with a reason from God's own character, that they have no regard for the works of the LORD. The repetition of 'hands' links the three sections: David lifts his hands in verse 2, the wicked have hands that have acted in verse 4, and God's hands are the works they ignore in verse 5.

The final section widens the prayer from one man to a nation. The 'I' of verses 1 to 7 becomes 'His people' in verses 8 and 9, and the shepherd, an image from the everyday life of the flocks, closes the poem with a picture of care that covers time as well as need: 'carry them forever.'
context.historical:
The psalm is headed 'of David' and reads like a prayer from a time when the king felt the threat of both open and hidden enemies. It contains no historical details, which is part of its usefulness. The phrase 'those descending to the Pit' belongs to the common Hebrew picture of the grave and the realm of the dead, Psalm 30:3 and Psalm 143:7, a place from which there is no praise and no answer. To be like them is to be beyond help.

The lifted hands of verse 2 describe the ordinary posture of prayer in Israel. The hands were spread out with the palms up, toward the sanctuary, Psalm 141:2, and Solomon's dedication prayer pictures people praying toward the temple, 1 Kings 8:38. The 'holy sanctuary' of verse 2 is the inner room, the most holy place, where the ark stood, and to lift the hands toward it is to pray in the direction of the throne of God.

The enemies of verse 3 use a specific weapon: they 'speak peace to their neighbors while malice is in their hearts.' In a society that ran on hospitality, oaths and greetings, the word 'peace' was both a blessing and a signal of trust. A false peace was therefore a betrayal of the very custom that held communities together, and the prophet Jeremiah made the same complaint, Jeremiah 9:8. In a court the flattery of a rival could be more dangerous than a threat.

The closing prayer for the anointed and for the people has a national and liturgical ring. The king was 'the anointed' by the act of oil, and Israel prayed for him in worship, Psalm 20:6. The image of the shepherd was central to how Israel understood both its kings and its God, Psalm 80:1, Ezekiel 34:23. Later Christian liturgy took over verse 9, 'Save Your people and bless Your inheritance', in a prayer that is still sung in many churches, showing how the line was heard as a prayer for the whole gathered people.
context.canonical:
The psalm has close neighbours in the Psalter. Psalm 143:7 uses the same fear, 'Do not hide Your face from me, or I will be like those who descend to the Pit,' and Psalm 35:22 says, 'O LORD, You have seen it; be not silent.' Psalm 83:1 asks that God not be silent or still. The cry that God not be deaf is one of the standard prayers of the sufferer, and the answer is regularly given as a rescue from the Pit, Psalm 30:3.

The picture of the hypocrite who speaks smoothly is also repeated. Psalm 12:2 has 'flattering lips and a double heart', Psalm 55:21 has words 'softer than oil, yet they are swords unsheathed', and Jeremiah 9:8 has a man who speaks peace to his neighbor and sets a trap in his heart. These texts together form a small theology of deceit that reaches its climax in Judas's kiss, Luke 22:47 to 48.

The prayer for repayment is complemented in the New Testament by a warning against taking it into our own hands. Paul quotes 'Vengeance is Mine; I will repay,' and tells believers not to avenge themselves, Romans 12:19, and he says of a man who did him great harm that 'The Lord will repay him according to his deeds,' 2 Timothy 4:14, using the language of Psalm 28:4 while leaving the matter with God. Jesus tells His followers to love their enemies and pray for them, Matthew 5:44, and from the cross He asks forgiveness for those who crucify Him, Luke 23:34.

The closing images echo the Old Testament story of Israel. God carried His people 'as a man carries his son', Deuteronomy 1:31, and 'lifted them up and carried them all the days of old', Isaiah 63:9; He calls them His allotted inheritance, Deuteronomy 32:9. The shepherd figure returns in the promise of one shepherd, David, Ezekiel 34:23, and in the New Testament Jesus is 'the good shepherd', John 10:11, and 'that great Shepherd of the sheep', Hebrews 13:20. In Revelation the Lamb at the centre of the throne becomes their shepherd, Revelation 7:17.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
David wants his hearers to learn that prayer is a dependency on the voice of God. The first thing he fears is silence. Every other trouble in the psalm, the enemies, the deceit and the danger of the Pit, is secondary to the possibility that God will not answer. He intends Israel to understand that a life without an answer from God is a life already sliding toward the grave, and that the whole point of the sanctuary is that God can be spoken to.

He also means to correct a temptation. When the wicked are polished and friendly, it is easy to trust their words or to fear their power. David wants the worshipper to look at the heart, at what someone is planning, and to ask God to deal with it. He commits the payback to God, not to his own hand, and he offers the ground of it: they show no regard for what the LORD has done.

The change in verse 6 is meant to teach. The psalmist does not wait for the outward situation to be repaired before he praises. He praises because he has been heard, and the point is the hearing itself. The last verses widen the prayer so that the reader does not finish the psalm alone. The person who has been helped is expected to pray for the king and the whole people, for their safety and for their being carried. The first hearers were meant to learn to pass from private need to public intercession.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm records what David prayed. Its request in verse 4 that God repay the wicked is a prayer, not an instruction to take revenge, and it is addressed to God, who alone is entitled to judge. It is therefore descriptive of a right way to bring anger into prayer, and it cannot be treated as a licence for personal vengeance. The New Testament shows that the same words are placed in God's hands, Romans 12:19, and then softened by the command to love enemies, Matthew 5:44. A believer can pray for justice and pray for the enemy's repentance at once, since God's justice includes the possibility of forgiveness in Christ.

The claim of verse 5, that God will tear them down and never rebuild them, is a statement of what happens to those who despise God's works, not a threat that believers are to carry out. It is a promise about His judgment.

What does carry across to us directly is the pattern of prayer. We bring the fear that God will be silent, we lift our hands, and we thank Him before the outward change. The closing intercession, 'Save Your people and bless Your inheritance', is also a prayer the church can pray for its leaders and for one another, 1 Timothy 2:1 to 2, without needing to attach the specifics of David's kingdom.

debates.question: What explains the sudden change from petition to praise between verses 5 and 6?

views.label: A word of assurance from God, perhaps through a priest or prophet, came between the two halves
views.case: Some scholars suggest that a person in trouble would pray in the sanctuary and then receive an oracle of salvation, after which the mood changes. The perfect tense 'He has heard' in verse 6 would then respond to something that has been said, though the psalm does not record it.

views.label: Confidence spoken in advance
views.case: The Hebrew perfect can describe something so certain that it is spoken of as already done. David is so sure of being heard that he thanks God before the outward change. The praise is therefore an act of faith, not a response to news.

views.label: Two prayers joined together, a lament and a later thanksgiving
views.case: Others hold that the psalm was made from a lament and a hymn of thanks, brought together by the community, so that a prayer offered in danger was completed by a song offered after deliverance.

debates.bearing: Whichever explanation is preferred, the psalm teaches the same thing: being heard by God, not the removal of every threat, is what turns fear into song. The silence between the verses is part of the lesson.

debates.question: Is the prayer for repayment in verse 4 consistent with Christian teaching about enemies?

views.label: Yes, it is a prayer for justice placed in God's hands
views.case: David does not act himself. He asks God to do what only God may do, and the New Testament uses the same language, 2 Timothy 4:14, while placing vengeance with God, Romans 12:19. The prayer is a way of giving up the right to retaliate.

views.label: It reflects the limits of the old covenant setting and is completed by the teaching of Jesus
views.case: The command to love enemies and to pray for persecutors, Matthew 5:44, and the prayer for forgiveness from the cross, Luke 23:34, take the reader beyond the spirit of verse 4. The psalm is honest but is not the final word.

views.label: It is a prophetic anticipation of final judgment
views.case: Because verse 5 speaks of the wicked being torn down and not rebuilt, some read the whole section as pointing to the last judgment, when God will repay every person's deeds, Revelation 22:12, so that the prayer is answered at the end of history.

debates.bearing: The readings do not compete as much as they layer. The psalm gives the believer permission to name evil and to ask God to deal with it, and the rest of Scripture keeps that prayer from turning into personal vengeance.

debates.question: Who is the 'anointed' of verse 8: David, the reigning king or the Messiah?

views.label: The reigning king of Israel
views.case: The Hebrew mashiach was the ordinary title for a king who had been anointed with oil, 1 Samuel 16:13, and Psalm 20:6 uses it in a prayer for a king. The prayer for people and king together fits the setting of national worship.

views.label: The king, who also points ahead to the Messiah
views.case: Because God's covenant with David promised an everlasting throne, 2 Samuel 7:16, the title carried a forward pressure, and Habakkuk 3:13 speaks of God going out 'to save Your anointed'. The New Testament takes the title to its fulfilment, Acts 2:36.

debates.bearing: The first hearers heard a prayer for their king. Christians, who confess that Jesus is the Anointed One, hear in the same words the promise of a king who does not fail.

study.originalLanguages:
The first verse is a play on two verbs of silence. The 'be not deaf' is from the root charash, which means to be silent or deaf, and 'if You remain silent' uses a related verb, chashah. David begs that the Rock not be deaf toward him. The word he uses for God, 'my Rock', is tsuri, the same word as Psalm 18:2, a mountain-cliff image of God who cannot be moved. The speaker is asking a rock to speak, and the request has a quiet boldness: what stands unmoved is asked to hear.

'Cry for mercy' in verse 2 is techinnah, named in the basic level, but the second word there is worth noticing, for the 'cry for help', shav'i, carries the sense of a call for rescue. David puts a word for mercy beside a word for rescue, and both are directed at the 'holy sanctuary', which is the Hebrew devir. The BSB footnote says 'Your innermost sanctuary or Your Most Holy Place', and the word devir is used for the innermost room of the temple, the room that held the ark, 1 Kings 6:5. David turns his hands toward the very room in which God's throne was placed.

Verse 3 has the phrase dovrei shalom, 'those who speak peace', an unusual one. The word shalom is the greeting and the covenant word for wholeness, and here it is a mask. Notice that the next psalm ends with God blessing His people with shalom, so the two psalms display the true and the false of the same word.

In verse 5 the wicked 'show no regard' for the works of the LORD. The Hebrew is lo yavinu, 'they do not discern or understand', from binah, the word for insight. They do not fail to see the works but fail to grasp what they mean. God's response is that He will 'tear them down and never rebuild them'. The two verbs, harats and banah, form a pair, and they are the same pair in Jeremiah 1:10 where God appoints the prophet to tear down and build up. God's tearing here is not followed by building.

The 'anointed' of verse 8 is the singular form of mashiach with a pronoun, 'His anointed', and the verse begins with a different reading in the manuscripts: the Hebrew says 'strength for them', and several ancient versions read 'for His people', which is how the BSB takes it. Verse 9 ends with two verbs that belong together, ra'ah, 'shepherd', and nasa, 'carry', the verb Moses used of God carrying Israel like a son, Deuteronomy 1:31. The word rendered 'inheritance' is nachalah, the property passed from a father to his heirs, the word for what Israel is to God in Deuteronomy 32:9. God's people are His estate.

typology.type: Lifted hands toward the innermost sanctuary, verse 2
typology.fulfillment: David prays toward the devir, the place where God was enthroned above the ark. In Christ the direction of prayer is changed, for the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom at His death, Matthew 27:51, and the believer has confidence to enter the holy places by His blood, Hebrews 10:19 to 20. Paul asks that men everywhere lift up holy hands in prayer, 1 Timothy 2:8. The type falls short because David could only lift his hands toward a room he could not enter; in Christ the way inside is opened.

typology.type: The anointed one saved and the people shepherded, verses 8 and 9
typology.fulfillment: The prayer that God would save His anointed and carry His people is answered in the Messiah. After the resurrection Peter declares that God has made Jesus 'both Lord and Christ', Acts 2:36, Christ meaning the Anointed One. The type falls short in that David's kings died and failed, whereas Jesus lives for ever, Hebrews 7:24 to 25, and the salvation of the anointed in Habakkuk 3:13 is worked out in the resurrection.

The verbs shepherd and carry are joined in Isaiah 40:11, where the LORD gathers lambs in His arms, and in Jesus who says, 'I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep,' John 10:11. Hebrews calls Him 'that great Shepherd of the sheep', brought back from the dead, Hebrews 13:20, and Peter says believers have returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of their souls, 1 Peter 2:25. The pattern is strengthened by the last book, where the Lamb is their shepherd, Revelation 7:17. The type falls short at the cost: David's shepherds guarded, but Christ's shepherd gave his life.

typology.type: Not descending to the Pit, verse 1
typology.fulfillment: The fear of David is the fear of the grave. In the Gospel it is what Christ went through, and He was not held by it, Acts 2:24. He descended, was buried and rose, and He says, 'I was dead, and behold, now I am alive forever and ever!' Revelation 1:18. Those who are in Him will not be abandoned to the Pit. The type falls short because David could only pray for exemption; Christ went through death and made it a way out.

study.christ:
Psalm 28 leads to Christ by the title in its final lines. The 'anointed' of verse 8 is the Hebrew mashiach, and the New Testament word for it is Christ. On the day of Pentecost Peter says that 'God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ,' Acts 2:36. David prays that the LORD would be a stronghold of salvation for His anointed, and the Gospel announces that the Anointed has been saved from death and set at the right hand of God. In the psalm's own terms the prayer is answered: God 'heard' the cry, and the Anointed was raised.

It leads to Christ by the picture of a shepherd who carries. The last verse asks God to shepherd and carry His people, and every part of the picture is fulfilled in Jesus. He says 'I am the good shepherd', John 10:11, He knows His sheep, and He says they will never perish and no one will snatch them from His hand, John 10:27 to 28. The writer to the Hebrews names Him 'that great Shepherd of the sheep', Hebrews 13:20, and Revelation says He will lead them to springs of living water, Revelation 7:17. The word 'forever' in verse 9 is answered by the eternal covenant of Hebrews 13:20.

It leads to Christ by the cry that God not be silent. The psalmist fears the Pit if God does not speak, and Jesus went into that very silence. On the cross He cried, 'My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?' Matthew 27:46, quoting Psalm 22:1, and He gave a loud voice at the end and yielded up His spirit. The Father's answer came on the third day, in the raising of the Son, Acts 2:24. The prayer 'be not deaf to me, O my Rock' is a prayer that only the resurrection fully answers, and the same rescue is the promise for all who are in Him.

The prayer for repayment also meets Christ in an unexpected way. David asks that the wicked be repaid for what their hands have done; the cross is where the payment for the hands of sinners fell on the sinless one. Peter says that He 'bore our sins in His body on the tree', 1 Peter 2:24, and the wickedness that the psalmist wanted judged is judged there, so that those who trust Him are not repaid according to their deeds.

A caution is in order. Not every detail of the psalm is a hidden portrait of Jesus, and the prayer for retribution cannot be placed on His lips without the qualification of His own prayer, 'Father, forgive them,' Luke 23:34. The links that the apostles draw are the anointed, the shepherd and the rescue from the Pit, and those links are strong enough.
study.god:
Psalm 28 begins with a God who speaks and hears, and everything follows from that. The psalmist can only fear God's silence because God is a God who answers. A God who did not speak would not be dreaded. The complaint 'be not deaf to me' assumes that His hearing is the ordinary way that He treats His people, and the confidence of verse 6, 'He has heard my cry for mercy', shows that it is.

God is a rock, a strength and a shield. Each title adds something. The rock is the unmoved ground; the strength is what He gives, and the shield is what stands between David and the blow. The psalm does not say the LORD gives strength, it says the LORD is his strength, verse 7, so the gift is Himself. The trust in the heart, 'I am helped', is followed by rejoicing, and the doctrine of God is turned at once into worship.

He is a God who sees the heart and who judges hidden malice. The people of verse 3 keep the surface clean, but God cares about what is planned in the heart. His justice does not wait for a visible crime; it attends to the intent, and it corresponds to the work: 'according to their deeds.' The psalm also gives a reason for that judgment: they have no regard for the works of the LORD or what His hands have done. The offence at the root is a refusal to perceive God, and the sentence is that God will tear down what such people build.

He is a God who shepherds. The image at the end is of a Lord who holds the whole flock, 'Your people' and 'Your inheritance'. The people are both the flock He cares for and the possession that He treasures. To carry them for ever is to promise that His care will last as long as the flock. This is one of the tenderest pictures of God in the Psalter, and it stands beside the fierce language of verses 4 and 5 without contradiction. The one who tears down the wicked is the one who carries the weak.

He is also a God who is honoured in the song of the person He has helped. 'I give thanks to Him with my song' is the way verse 7 closes. For worship this means that we come first as those in need, lifting our hands, and leave as those who have been heard, with praise that is fitted to what He has done. We can pray for justice, and we can pray for His people, and we can trust the Rock who has promised to hear.

crossReferences.note: 'Do not hide Your face from me, or I will be like those who descend to the Pit.' The same dread as Psalm 28:1 in another psalm of David. The two show that the fear of God's silence was not a passing mood but a persistent shape of his prayer.

'O LORD, You pulled me up from Sheol; You spared me from descending into the Pit.' This is the answer to the fear of Psalm 28:1, given in a thanksgiving song, and it shows how the prayer not to go down to the Pit is granted.

A man speaks peace to his neighbor with his mouth but sets a trap in his heart. Psalm 28:3 describes the same deceit, and the prophet confirms that this smooth betrayal was a common scandal in Israel and a target of God's judgment.

'They lie to one another; they speak with flattering lips and a double heart.' The double heart is the exact condition David describes in the workers of iniquity of Psalm 28:3, and Psalm 12 goes on to say that the LORD will rise up on behalf of the needy.

'Vengeance is Mine; I will repay, says the Lord.' Paul takes the principle that lies behind Psalm 28:4 and applies it to the church: the believer leaves repayment to God. It shows how the psalm's prayer is to be read in the light of the gospel.

Paul says that Alexander did him great harm and that the Lord will repay him according to his deeds. It is a New Testament echo of Psalm 28:4, showing that even the apostle trusted the matter to God rather than acting himself.

'May my prayer be set before You like incense, my uplifted hands like the evening offering.' The uplifted hands of Psalm 28:2 are here compared to a sacrifice, showing that the physical posture of prayer was understood as an offering in itself.

The LORD carried His people in the wilderness 'as a man carries his son'. The verb of Psalm 28:9, carry, is drawn from this history, and the prayer asks that what God did in the desert may be done for ever.

God promises to carry His people from the womb to old age, 'I have made you, and I will carry you.' It is the closest prophetic parallel to the 'forever' of Psalm 28:9 and shows that the promised carrying is a lifelong commitment.

God went out for the salvation of His people, 'to save Your anointed'. It pairs the same two objects as Psalm 28:8, people and anointed, and pictures God's saving work as a campaign for both together.

'I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep.' Jesus places Himself in the role of the LORD who shepherds in Psalm 28:9 and adds the note that the care of the shepherd will cost His life.

The Lamb at the centre of the throne will be the shepherd of His people and lead them to living water. It is the final form of the prayer that God would shepherd and carry His people, and it shows that the prayer's 'forever' has a destination.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 28 stands in the story where God's people depend on His speaking. At creation He spoke and there was light, Genesis 1:3, and in the garden He spoke to the man and the woman and walked with them. The fall was a moment when His word was doubted and His presence was lost. From then on the Bible's characters cry out for a God who will speak again, and Psalm 28 is one of those cries. The fear of God's silence is the fear of the world outside the garden, where the voice is no longer heard face to face.

The psalm also places the problem of evil within that story. The wicked of verse 3 are not simply outsiders; they speak peace and have a heart of malice, and they show the same kind of deceit as the serpent, who offered a word that sounded kind while it destroyed. David asks God to deal with that hidden evil. The answer will come in stages: in the judgments of the prophets, in the crushing of the serpent's head, Genesis 3:15, and in the cross, where God bears the weight of it Himself.

The last verses look forward to the shepherd-king. From Genesis, where Jacob speaks of God who has shepherded him all his life, Genesis 48:15, through Moses' picture of a God who carried Israel, to David, who was a shepherd before he was a king, the image builds. The prophets promise one shepherd, Ezekiel 34:23, and Jesus arrives as the good shepherd, John 10:11. He is the Anointed for whom David prayed.

The story concludes in the presence of a God who never falls silent. In the new creation the voice from the throne says, 'Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man,' Revelation 21:3, and the Lamb shepherds His people to springs of living water, Revelation 7:17. The Pit is gone, for death will be no more, Revelation 21:4. The people who were once carried through the wilderness are carried home, and the cry 'be not deaf to me' is answered for ever by the God who speaks.

quiz.q: What does David fear will happen if God remains silent, according to verse 1?

options.text: He will become like those descending to the Pit.
options.note: David states this fear explicitly as the reason for his urgent cry.

options.text: He will suffer some unspecified misfortune.
options.note: Close, since misfortune is implied, but the verse names a specific fate, becoming like those descending to the Pit, not a vague, unspecified trouble.

options.text: He will be forgotten by his own family.
options.note: The verse concerns God's silence and its ultimate consequence, not family relationships.

options.text: He will grow old before his time.
options.note: The concern is spiritual and mortal, being like those going down to the Pit, not aging.

quiz.q: What description does David give of the wicked in verse 3?

options.text: They speak peace to their neighbors while malice is in their hearts.
options.note: This captures the specific hidden hypocrisy David prays against.

options.text: They openly declare war on their neighbors.
options.note: The text specifically highlights hidden malice behind peaceful speech, not open declarations of hostility.

options.text: They are simply unfriendly and cold toward their neighbors.
options.note: Close, since real hostility is present, but the verse specifically highlights deceptive peaceable speech masking malice, not mere coldness.

options.text: They openly confess their wrongdoing.
options.note: This is the opposite; they conceal malice behind peaceable words rather than confessing it.

quiz.q: What happens to David's tone starting in verse 6?

options.text: It shifts to praise, blessing the LORD for hearing his cry for mercy.
options.note: Verse 6 marks a clear turn from plea to thanksgiving.

options.text: It becomes calmer but remains uncertain whether God has answered.
options.note: Close, since the tone does shift, but verse 6 states outright confidence, 'Blessed be the LORD, for He has heard,' not lingering uncertainty.

options.text: It returns to describing his fear of the Pit.
options.note: The tone moves forward into praise, not backward into fear.

options.text: It becomes a plea for more specific instructions.
options.note: The shift in verse 6 is thanksgiving for being heard, not a request for further instruction.

quiz.q: What two titles does David give the LORD in verse 7?

options.text: His strength and his shield.
options.note: David explicitly names the LORD as his strength and his shield in this verse.

options.text: His helper and his refuge.
options.note: Close in meaning, since strength and shield imply help and refuge, but verse 7 uses the specific titles strength and shield, not these synonyms.

options.text: His enemy and his rival.
options.note: This is the opposite of the trusting relationship described in the verse.

options.text: His servant and his subject.
options.note: The verse describes the LORD as David's strength and shield, not in a servant role to David.

quiz.q: What does David ask God to do for His people and His anointed in verses 8-9?

options.text: Save them, bless them, shepherd them, and carry them forever.
options.note: This closing intercession widens David's personal deliverance into prayer for the whole people and their anointed king.

options.text: Give them greater military strength alone.
options.note: While strength is mentioned, the specific closing prayer is for salvation, blessing, shepherding, and carrying, a broader and more relational hope.

options.text: Simply leave them to fend for themselves without further involvement.
options.note: Close in that God's active help is the topic, but this option reverses the plea, which asks for ongoing, active shepherding and carrying, not withdrawal.

options.text: Punish them for their past failures.
options.note: The prayer is one of blessing and care, not punishment.

questions: David fears becoming like those descending to the Pit if God remains silent. What does your own prayer life look like when you feel God is silent, do you press in or pull away?

David prays against those who speak peace while hiding malice in their hearts. Where have you experienced, or perhaps practiced, this kind of hidden hypocrisy, and how does this psalm call you to honesty instead?

The psalm turns from urgent plea to confident praise the moment David knows he has been heard. What unanswered prayer are you currently carrying, and how might trusting that God hears change your posture while you wait?

David closes by praying not just for himself but for God's anointed king and all God's people. Who in your church or community can you intercede for today, widening your prayers beyond your own needs?
The psalm's closing image is of God shepherding and carrying His people forever. Where in your life do you most need to be carried right now rather than expected to walk under your own strength?

translationNotes.note: The Pit is a common Old Testament image for the grave or Sheol, the realm of the dead, used here to express the gravity of unanswered prayer.
Lifting up hands toward the sanctuary was a customary posture of prayer, oriented toward God's dwelling place even from a distance.
Anointed renders mashiach, the title for Israel's set-apart king, later applied supremely to Jesus as God's ultimate Anointed One, or Christ.
